CausalChain: Cardiac stress -> mitochondrial dysfunction in cardiomyocytes -> increased production of specific mtlncRNAs (e.g., LIPCAR) -> selective packaging into exosomes -> exosome release into extracellular milieu -> uptake by neighboring cardiomyocytes -> modulation of nuclear lncRNA networks -> reactivation of cardioprotective gene expression -> improved tissue repair
Hypothesis: Mitochondrial lncRNAs generated under cardiac stress are actively packaged into exosomes and transferred to neighboring cells, where they modulate nuclear lncRNA regulatory networks to activate cardioprotective and repair pathways during heart failure.
Abstract: Cardiac stress invariably induces adaptive signaling mechanisms to ameliorate tissue damage, yet the precise molecular mediators orchestrating these responses remain incompletely defined. Here we propose a novel mechanism whereby mitochondrial long non‐coding RNAs (mtlncRNAs), generated in stressed cardiomyocytes, are selectively packaged into exosomes and released, serving as intercellular messengers. Upon uptake by neighboring cardiac cells, these mtlncRNAs modulate the transcriptional regulatory network of nuclear-localized lncRNAs, thereby activating cardioprotective gene expression and promoting repair mechanisms. This abstract hypothesis integrates mitochondrial dysfunction, exosome-mediated lncRNA exchange, and subsequent nuclear reprogramming as a unified adaptive response in heart failure, paving the way for innovative diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.
